result: TMSC transplantation significantly reduced intraocular pressure (IOP) in Tg-MyocY437H mice. Day-time IOP decreased from 16.5±0.44 mmHg at baseline to 13.30±0.42 mmHg at 1 month and 12.65±0.36 mmHg at 2 months post-transplantation, reaching levels comparable to wild-type mice. Night IOP similarly normalized from 17.73±2.25 mmHg to 11.75±2.83 mmHg.
evaluation: Claims C31-C41 provide comprehensive IOP measurements with appropriate statistical comparisons (p-values reported), adequate sample sizes (n=26 per group), proper controls (WT, Tg, Tg-Sham), and measurements at multiple time points. The data demonstrate statistically significant IOP reduction with TMSC treatment compared to untreated and sham controls, with no significant difference from WT mice.

result: TMSC transplantation increased outflow facility in Tg-MyocY437H mice. Outflow facility improved from 0.010±0.001 μL/min/mmHg in untreated Tg mice to 0.016±0.002 μL/min/mmHg after TMSC treatment, approaching the level of WT mice (0.017±0.001 μL/min/mmHg), indicating restoration of conventional outflow pathway function.
evaluation: Claims C42-C46 present outflow facility measurements with appropriate statistical analysis (p=0.0487 vs Tg, p=0.029 vs Tg-Sham), adequate sample size (n=6 eyes/group), and proper controls. The R² values >0.95 for flow rate measurements indicate reliable data quality. The mechanistic link to TM-Schlemm's canal pathway is appropriately inferred from the conventional outflow measurement method.

result: Corneal thickness was uniform across all experimental groups, and no anterior synechia was observed following TMSC or sham injection, confirming that IOP measurements were not confounded by corneal changes and that the injection procedure did not cause adverse structural complications.
evaluation: Claims C47-C48 are supported by OCT measurements (Figure 1D-E) with adequate sample size (n=8 eyes/group). These control measurements are essential for validating IOP measurement accuracy and demonstrating safety of the intracameral injection procedure.

result: TMSC transplantation preserved retinal ganglion cell (RGC) function and prevented RGC loss in Tg-MyocY437H mice. PERG measurements showed that ~90% of RGC function was preserved (P1 amplitude: 9.20±0.45 μV in Tg-TMSC vs 10.84±0.86 μV in WT, p=0.1934), compared to only 60% in untreated Tg mice. RGC counts increased from 49.22±1.79 cells/mm in untreated Tg mice to 60.60±1.25 cells/mm with TMSC treatment.
evaluation: Claims C49-C55 provide convergent evidence from both functional (PERG) and structural (cell counting) assessments with appropriate statistical analysis, adequate sample sizes (n=10 eyes for PERG, n=4-6 eyes with 12-16 sections for counting), and proper controls. The consistency between functional preservation and structural protection strengthens the conclusion.

result: TMSC transplantation significantly increased trabecular meshwork (TM) cellularity in Tg-MyocY437H mice. TM cell density increased from 20.33±1.11 cells/section in untreated Tg mice (42% reduction from WT) to 28.86±1.46 cells/section with TMSC treatment (p=0.0028), partially restoring the cellularity toward WT levels (35.33±2.50 cells/section).
evaluation: Claims C56-C59 present TM cellularity data with appropriate quantification methods (collagen IV staining to define TM region), adequate sample size (n=10-14 sections/group), statistical analysis, and proper controls. The partial restoration of cellularity is consistent with the functional improvements in IOP and outflow facility.

result: Transplanted TMSCs integrated into the TM tissue and differentiated into cells expressing TM markers (AQP1 and CHI3L1). Some transplanted cells were Ki67-positive, indicating active proliferation at 2 months post-transplantation. TUNEL staining showed that transplanted TMSCs remained viable and appeared to protect endogenous TM cells from apoptosis.
evaluation: Claims C60-C62, C97 are supported by immunofluorescent staining and TUNEL analysis (Figure 4) showing DiO-labeled TMSCs expressing TM markers, proliferation markers, and reduced apoptosis. The data demonstrate successful engraftment and differentiation, though the proportion of differentiated cells is not quantified.

result: TMSC transplantation promoted myocilin secretion from TM cells into the aqueous humor in Tg-MyocY437H mice. Myocilin protein levels decreased in limbal tissue and dramatically increased in aqueous humor following TMSC treatment, suggesting enhanced secretion of the mutant protein rather than its intracellular accumulation.
evaluation: Claims C63-C69 are supported by immunofluorescent staining (Figure 5A) and Western blotting (Figure 5B-C) with adequate sample sizes (n=5) and statistical analysis. The reciprocal changes in tissue vs. aqueous humor myocilin levels provide strong evidence for enhanced secretion. However, the mechanism by which TMSCs promote secretion is not elucidated.

result: TMSC transplantation remodeled extracellular matrix (ECM) components in the TM tissue of Tg-MyocY437H mice. Fibronectin and elastin levels, which were elevated in untreated Tg mice, were reduced to WT levels following TMSC treatment, while collagen IV remained unchanged.
evaluation: Claims C70-C73 are supported by Western blotting data (Figure 5D) with adequate sample sizes (n=4-6) and statistical analysis showing significant normalization of fibronectin and elastin. The selective modulation of specific ECM components is consistent with restoration of TM homeostasis.

result: TMSC transplantation partially ameliorated ER stress in Tg-MyocY437H mice. While ER stress markers (CHOP and GRP78) in limbal tissue were not significantly reduced, TEM analysis showed that ER lumen size decreased from 24.53±2.81 nm²/nm in untreated Tg mice to 13.78±1.02 nm²/nm with TMSC treatment (p=0.049), approaching WT levels (7.03±0.54 nm²/nm).
evaluation: Claims C74-C78 present mixed results: Western blotting shows no significant reduction in ER stress markers, but TEM analysis demonstrates significant ultrastructural improvement. The discrepancy may reflect different sensitivities of the methods or heterogeneity in the tissue response. The ultrastructural data provide more direct evidence of ER stress reduction at the cellular level.

result: TMSC transplantation resulted in ultrastructural restoration of TM tissue, with many cells displaying normal ultrastructure without swollen ER in the TM region of Tg-MyocY437H mice.
evaluation: Claims C9 and C114 are supported by TEM data (Figure 6B-C) showing reduced ER swelling and improved cellular ultrastructure. The quantitative ER size measurements (C76-C78) provide objective support for the qualitative ultrastructural observations.

result: TMSCs did not stimulate proliferation of mutant TM cells in vitro. EdU incorporation rates were similar whether mutant TM cells were cultured alone (6.53±1.19%), co-cultured with TMSCs in Transwell inserts (6.06±1.78%, p=0.8267), or in direct contact with TMSCs (6.51±1.63%, p=0.9932).
evaluation: Claims C79-C82 are supported by EdU incorporation and flow cytometry data (Figure 7D) with adequate replication (n=3-5) and appropriate statistical analysis showing no significant differences. This negative result is important for understanding the mechanism of TM cellularity increase observed in vivo.

result: TMSCs did not reverse ER stress in cultured MyocY437H mutant TM cells. Co-culturing TM cells with TMSCs in Transwell inserts had little effect on reducing expression of ER stress markers (GRP78, CHOP) or promoting myocilin secretion in the mutant TM cells.
evaluation: Claims C83-C85, C102 are supported by Western blotting data (Figure 7E-F) with adequate replication (n=3). This negative result in vitro contrasts with the in vivo improvements, suggesting that the therapeutic mechanism may involve factors not captured in the Transwell co-culture system, such as cell-cell contact, three-dimensional tissue architecture, or other cell types.

result: Co-culturing TMSCs with myocilin mutant TM cells in vitro promoted TMSC differentiation into functional TM cells. TMSCs co-cultured with normal or mutant TM cells showed increased CHI3L1 expression, became responsive to dexamethasone treatment (increased myocilin expression), and gained phagocytic function.
evaluation: Claims C86-C89 are supported by Western blotting (Figure 8B-C) and phagocytosis assays (Figure 8D-E) with adequate replication (n=3 for Western blots, n=10 fields for phagocytosis). The data demonstrate that TMSCs can differentiate into TM-like cells even under ER stress conditions, supporting the in vivo differentiation observed.

result: RNA sequencing revealed that TMSCs had upregulated genes related to TM regeneration compared to fibroblasts. Upregulated genes included those involved in TM ECM maintenance, integrity, and motility (ITGA3, CHI3L1, VTN, LOX, FST, COL4A6), with enrichment in focal adhesion, PI3K-Akt signaling, and ECM-receptor interaction pathways.
evaluation: Claims C90-C93 are supported by RNA sequencing data (Figure 9A) from three independent TMSC and fibroblast strains with appropriate bioinformatic analysis (FDR<1%, p<0.01). The pathway analysis provides mechanistic insights into TMSC regenerative capacity. However, validation of key differentially expressed genes by qRT-PCR or other methods would strengthen the conclusions.

result: RNA sequencing and pathway analysis identified upregulation of genes and pathways related to neuroprotection in TMSCs. These included genes involved in synapse formation and function (NEURL1, neurofascin, neuroligins), proteins in glutamatergic, dopaminergic, and GABAergic pathways, and enrichment of neurotrophin and PI3K-Akt signaling pathways.
evaluation: Claims C94-C96 are supported by RNA sequencing data and pathway analysis (Figure 9B). The identification of neuroprotective gene expression provides a potential mechanism for RGC protection. However, functional validation of neuroprotective effects through paracrine signaling would be needed to confirm this mechanism.

result: TMSC transplantation led to multiple coordinated improvements in TM tissue: increased cellularity, reduced ECM components (fibronectin and elastin), enhanced myocilin secretion, decreased intracellular myocilin accumulation, and improved cellular ultrastructure. These changes collectively suggest that differentiated healthy TM cells from TMSCs replaced mutant TM cells and remodeled the ECM, improving TM tissue function.
evaluation: Claims C98-C101, C113-C115 synthesize multiple experimental findings into a coherent mechanistic model. The individual components are well-supported by data, and the integrated interpretation is reasonable. However, C115 includes speculative elements about cell replacement that are not directly demonstrated (e.g., no lineage tracing to confirm replacement vs. rescue of endogenous cells).

result: RNA sequencing analysis showing upregulation of genes related to TM regeneration in TMSCs compared to fibroblasts may explain the regenerative capacity of TMSCs. TMSCs and fibroblasts are distinctive in biological characteristics, with TMSCs expressing higher levels of genes involved in ECM modulation, TM integrity, and motility, including CHI3L1 and integrins.
evaluation: Claims C103-C104, C125-C127, C130 integrate RNA sequencing data with functional observations and prior work. The comparative analysis with fibroblasts (which lack regenerative capacity) strengthens the interpretation. However, C103 and C127 contain speculative elements about mechanisms that require further validation.

result: The study concludes that transplanted TMSCs can integrate into TM tissue, differentiate into functional TM cells, repopulate the TM, remodel ECM, restore TM homeostasis and outflow facility, reduce IOP, and preserve RGCs and their function in the Tg-MyocY437H mouse model of POAG. Restoration of TM cellularity and ECM remodeling are proposed as crucial mechanisms for cell-based glaucoma therapy.
evaluation: Claims C117 and C134 represent the main conclusions synthesizing all experimental findings. The conclusions are well-supported by the comprehensive dataset including IOP measurements, outflow facility, RGC function and counts, TM cellularity, ECM analysis, and differentiation studies. The mechanistic insights are appropriately qualified as inferences based on the data.

result: Background claims establish that glaucoma is a leading cause of irreversible blindness, POAG is the most common type (prevalence 0.5-7.0% in adults), and elevated IOP in POAG is associated with reduced TM cellularity, malfunction of TM phagocytosis, and abnormal ECM deposition.
evaluation: Claims C1, C12-C17 present established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to published literature. These provide the scientific rationale for the study.

result: Background claims establish that TMSCs have been isolated and characterized, maintain stem cell properties after cryopreservation, preferentially home to TM tissue after intracameral injection, and can improve outflow facility in laser-induced TM damage models.
evaluation: Claims C18-C23 present prior work on TMSCs supported by appropriate citations, including the authors' previous publications. These establish the foundation for testing TMSCs in a genetic POAG model.

result: Background claims establish that POAG pathogenesis differs from laser-induced glaucoma, myocilin mutations are associated with glaucoma (4% adult-onset, 10% juvenile-onset POAG), mutant myocilin accumulates in the ER causing ER stress, and the Tg-MyocY437H mouse model closely mimics human Myoc-associated glaucoma pathophysiology.
evaluation: Claims C24-C30 present established knowledge about myocilin-associated glaucoma and the mouse model, supported by appropriate citations. These justify the choice of the Tg-MyocY437H model for testing TMSC therapy.

result: Discussion claims establish that TMSCs respond differently to ER stress than TM cells, can differentiate into TM cells in normal and damaged TM tissue, and that TM homeostasis is important for IOP regulation. ER stress from mutant myocilin disrupts ECM assembly, leading to excessive ECM accumulation that further aggravates ER stress in a negative feedback loop.
evaluation: Claims C105-C112 synthesize prior work (supported by citations) with the current findings to provide mechanistic context. The claims appropriately distinguish between established knowledge and the current study's contributions.

result: Discussion claims compare the current findings to prior work showing that iPSC-derived TM cells and mesenchymal stem cells can reduce IOP, note that RGC preservation is as important as IOP reduction for glaucoma treatment, and speculate that the 10% RGC function loss may be due to delayed TMSC effect on IOP.
evaluation: Claims C116-C124 appropriately contextualize the findings within the broader literature and provide reasonable speculation about the partial RGC function loss. C119 and C124 are clearly identified as speculation.

result: Discussion claims establish that CHI3L1 and integrins are important for TM function and regeneration, and that genes identified in TMSC transcriptome (CACNA1A, KCNJ5) are involved in neuronal communication and neuroprotection. The authors speculate that RGC preservation is mainly due to reduced IOP, but neuroprotective proteins secreted by TMSCs might also contribute.
evaluation: Claims C128-C133 appropriately integrate RNA sequencing findings with functional outcomes and prior literature. C133 is clearly identified as speculation and appropriately qualified, acknowledging that IOP reduction is likely the primary mechanism.

result: The authors conclude that glaucoma with Myoc Y437H mutation shares common POAG pathophysiology (reduced TM cellularity, abnormal ECM, elevated IOP, RGC damage), and that these results open an avenue for stem-cell-based therapy for human open-angle glaucoma.
evaluation: Claims C135-C136 provide appropriate concluding statements. C135 correctly identifies the shared pathophysiology between Myoc mutation glaucoma and general POAG. C136 appropriately frames the translational potential while acknowledging this is a mouse model study.
